- If sentiment is consistently neutral or negative (0.00), model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 2–5% for next period.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model often overshoots; cap forecast at 10–15% above peak or use exponential decay to smooth.
- When sentiment shows early positive signals (e.g., >0.20), model frequently underestimates; adjust upward by 3–7% if sentiment >0.20 and price is falling.
- If model shows steady upward trend with no sentiment change, consider mean reversion; reduce slope by 10–20% if price has been rising >30% over 5 days.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows strong downward trend after peak, model often fails to recognize it; apply downward bias of 5–10% if sentiment remains flat or negative.
- If sentiment history includes multiple 0.00 entries followed by a spike, model tends to overreact; dampen forecast by 5–10% after the spike.
- When sentiment is positive but price is falling, model often ignores sentiment; if sentiment >0.20 and price is declining, reduce forecast by 3–8% to align with sentiment.
- For 30-day forecasts with high volatility, model often fails to capture mean reversion; apply a 1–3% downward correction if price has been above 90% of 30-day average for 3+ days.
